a female given name
Oda.et: Short form of female compound names beginning with the Germanic element ot "riches"; cognate with Old Norse Auðr (whence Icelandic Auður and Faroese Eyð/Eyður).

s: ode, poem of a certain type
Oder (a major river in the Czech Republic, Poland and Germany)
Oder.et: From Middle High German Odere, from Old High German Odera (in Latin texts; also attested as Oddara and various other forms). Further origin unknown, but usually considered Indo-European. Udolph connects it with Avestan 𐬀𐬛𐬎 (adu, “watercourse”), which is ultima…

s: or
Danach alles gestr. oder noch 1–2 Wörter?
Is everything after that crossed out or are there one or two more words?
oder.et: From Middle High German oder (whence also Yiddish אָדער (oder)), from Old High German odar, an alteration of odo by analogy with wedar (whence modern weder). The form odo is an assimilated, unstressed form of eddo (also edo), itself cognate with Old Saxon etth…

s: right?; is it?; is it not?

oder.et: From Middle High German oder (whence also Yiddish אָדער (oder)), from Old High German odar, an alteration of odo by analogy with wedar (whence modern weder). The form odo is an assimilated, unstressed form of eddo (also edo), itself cognate with Old Saxon etth…

s: badlands, wasteland
empty, bare, barren, bleak, desolate, deserted

tedious, dull, dreary
colloquial
Die Party wurde öde, also ging ich.
The party became boring so I left.

öde.et: From Middle High German œde, ōde, from Old High German ōdi, from Proto-West Germanic *auþī (“empty, barren”), from Proto-Germanic *auþijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewtyos (“forlorn, deserted”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ew (“away from”).

s: a mountain range in Hesse, Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg, Germany
Odenwald.et: From Old High German Odonewalt, Odanwalt, Otenwalt, a compound of walt (“forest”) (compare modern German Wald). The meaning of the first element is unknown; see Odenwald § Name for some hypotheses.

s: OR gate, a logic gate performing a Boolean logic OR operation
spirit, breath, life (in the sense of Biblical Hebrew רוֹחַ (rûaḥ))
poetic
Gott hat dem Menschen seinen Odem eingehaucht.

Psalm 150:6
Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah!
Odem.et: Central and Low German variant of Atem (“breath”) with the widespread dialectal development -ā- → -ō- and unshifted -d-; compare Middle Low German ādem. The form was spread through Luther’s Bible translation but did not replace the Upper German Atem in the eve…

s: wasteland
desertedness

Öde.et: From Old High German ōdi (“empty, deserted”), from Proto-West Germanic *auþī. Cognate to Old English ēaþe, īeþe and Old Norse auðr.

s: Oedipal
liquid manure
Odel.et: From Middle High German atel, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *adalaz. Cognate with English addle (“putrid”).

s: Oedipus
Ödipus.et: Borrowed from Latin Oedipūs, from Ancient Greek Οἰδίπους (Oidípous).
